evals.prompt: I just let an AI write this video transcription pipeline and I honestly don't get how choose_strategy decides between captions and ASR. Run /unvibe on this repo and help me actually own that logic. I'd say I'm only somewhat confident on it. Pick the most important piece, and go ahead and create the practice exercise files for me — yes, you can write to .unvibe/.
evals.expected_output: A shortlist of <=3 candidates, then a generated exercise under .unvibe/exercises/<YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS>_<slug>/ with a LeetCode-style README (Difficulty, happy-path Examples, Constraints, Signature), a Python stub, a pytest file with descriptive assertion messages and hidden edge/failure cases, and an executable run.sh.
expectations: The candidate shortlist presented to the user contains at most 3 items (1-3), with no filler/trivial candidates padded in to reach a number
A generated exercise directory exists whose name matches the timestamp format YYYY-MM-DD_HH-MM-SS_<slug> (date and time-with-seconds, underscore-separated, no colon character)

The exercise README.md is LeetCode-style: it includes a Difficulty label (EASY/MEDIUM/HARD), an Examples section with at least one concrete Input->Output pair, a Constraints section, and the function Signature
The README shows only happy-path examples; edge cases and failure/error cases are NOT spelled out in the README (they are left to the hidden tests)
An executable run.sh exists in the exercise directory; it runs the tests verbosely by default, accepts a -q flag for quiet mode, and accepts an optional single-test-name argument
The generated test file uses descriptive assertion messages so a failing test reports the case and expected-vs-actual, rather than only pass/fail
